claim: Dyslexia affects approximately 5% of the world's population.
source: Dyslexia, a specific and significant impairment in the development of reading skills that is not accounted for by mental age, visual acuity problems, or inadequate schooling (World Health Organization, 2016), affects ~5% of the world's population (Lindgren et al., 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lindgren et al., 1985.

claim: Individuals with dyslexia often have difficulties in simple non-linguistic perceptual tasks.
source: Though individuals with dyslexia are diagnosed for their reading impairments, they also often have difficulties in simple non-linguistic perceptual tasks (Mcanally and Stein, 1996; Ahissar et al., 2000; Sperling et al., 2005; Giraud and Ramus, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Perceptual difficulties in dyslexia can be largely explained as resulting from inefficient use of stimulus statistics that characterize the experiment.
source: These can be largely explained as resulting from inefficient use of stimulus statistics that characterize the experiment (the 'Anchoring Deficit hypothesis'; Ahissar et al., 2006; Oganian and Ahissar, 2012; Jaffe-Dax et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the Anchoring Deficit hypothesis and related studies.

claim: Perception tends to contract to the estimated mean of previous stimuli (contraction bias) when retention is required.
source: But their perception — in particular when retention is required, as for example in serial discrimination tasks — tends to contract to the estimated mean of previous stimuli (contraction bias; Raviv et al., 2012, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Raviv et al., 2012, 2014.

claim: The rate of decay of the behavioral effect of previous trials in serial discrimination is similar to the rate of decay of neural adaptation as measured by MEG.
source: Importantly, the rate of decay of the behavioral effect of previous trials in serial discrimination is similar to the rate of decay of neural adaptation, as measured by magnetoencephalography (MEG) (Lu et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 1992.

claim: Both the magnitude of perceptual contraction to the mean frequency of previous trials and the magnitude of neural adaptation decayed faster in participants with dyslexia.
source: Both the magnitude of perceptual contraction to the mean frequency of previous trials and the magnitude of neural adaptation (P2 and N1 components that are automatically produced by the auditory cortex [Mayhew et al., 2010]) decayed faster in participants with dyslexia (ERP [Jaffe-Dax et al., 2017]).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous ERP study (Jaffe-Dax et al., 2017).

claim: P2 and N1 components are automatically produced by the auditory cortex.
source: Both the magnitude of perceptual contraction to the mean frequency of previous trials and the magnitude of neural adaptation (P2 and N1 components that are automatically produced by the auditory cortex [Mayhew et al., 2010]) decayed faster in participants with dyslexia (ERP [Jaffe-Dax et al., 2017]).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mayhew et al., 2010.

claim: The study recruited 20 participants with dyslexia and 19 good readers from a previous study.
source: We recruited 20 participants with dyslexia and 19 good readers from our previous study (Table 1; Jaffe-Dax et al., 2017) and asked them to perform two-tone frequency discrimination in separate blocks with four trial-onset intervals (TOAs) of 3, 6, 9, and 15 s.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section and references Table 1 and the previous study.

claim: The two groups exhibited similar accuracy in the pre-scan training session (72.4 ± 6% vs. 73 ± 4.6%, z = 0.5, p=0.57).
source: The two groups exhibited similar accuracy (72.4 ± 6% vs. 73 ± 4.6%, z = 0.5, p=0.57).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical data from the study.

claim: In scans, good readers performed better than dyslexic participants (82.5 ± 1.6% vs. 76.3 ± 2.2%, z = 2.6, p<0.01).
source: In scans, good readers (controls) performed better than dyslexic participants (Mean ± SEM: 82.5 ± 1.6% vs. 76.3 ± 2.2%, z = 2.6, p<0.01 in Mann-Whitney U-tests), suggesting that they gained more from the short pre-scan practice (in line with the faster learning reported by Jaffe-Dax et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical data from the study.

claim: Good readers gained more from the short pre-scan practice than dyslexic participants.
source: In scans, good readers (controls) performed better than dyslexic participants (Mean ± SEM: 82.5 ± 1.6% vs. 76.3 ± 2.2%, z = 2.6, p<0.01 in Mann-Whitney U-tests), suggesting that they gained more from the short pre-scan practice (in line with the faster learning reported by Jaffe-Dax et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the performance difference and supported by citation to faster learning in Jaffe-Dax et al., 2017.

claim: Significant group differences in the whole-brain analysis were found in the left superior temporal lobe and in the right insular cortex.
source: Significant regions were found in the left superior temporal cortex (TAL: −54,–18, 10) and in the right insular cortex (TAL: 39,–2, −8), outlined in magenta in Figure 1A and 1B.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The superior temporal cortex is involved in a broad range of auditory tasks, including simple tone discrimination, language, and music.
source: The superior temporal cortex is known to be involved in a broad range of auditory tasks, including simple tone discrimination (Daikhin and Ahissar, 2015), language (Fedorenko et al., 2010) and music (Fedorenko et al., 2011), and even social tasks (e.g. Deen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The right insular cortex is multi-modal and is involved in introspection.
source: The right insular cortex is multi-modal (Bushara et al., 2003), and is also involved in introspection (Craig et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: BOLD activity in auditory regions was previously shown to correlate with the magnitude of N1–P2 responses.
source: BOLD activity in both auditory regions was previously shown to correlate with the magnitude of N1–P2 responses (Mayhew et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mayhew et al., 2010.

claim: The right insular cortex is probably not associated with the P2 response measured with ERP.
source: The right insular cortex is probably not associated with the P2 response that we measured with ERP and was therefore not predicted by our previous study.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the lack of association in previous ERP study.

claim: The general trend of shorter adaptation in participants with dyslexia was consistent across all responding voxels.
source: In addition, the general (though not significant) trend of shorter adaptation in participants with dyslexia was consistent across all responding voxels.
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis across all responding voxels.

claim: There is a broadly distributed tendency for shorter adaptation in dyslexia.
source: We found a broadly distributed tendency for shorter adaptation in dyslexia.
evidence: The claim is based on the fMRI data analysis presented in the study.

claim: The source of N1 was attributed to Planum Temporale in a seminal MEG study.
source: In a seminal MEG study (Lütkenhöner and Steinsträter, 1998), the source of N1 was attributed to Planum Temporale, and that of P2 to Heschl's gyrus.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lütkenhöner and Steinsträter, 1998.

claim: The source of P2 was attributed to Heschl's gyrus in a seminal MEG study.
source: In a seminal MEG study (Lütkenhöner and Steinsträter, 1998), the source of N1 was attributed to Planum Temporale, and that of P2 to Heschl's gyrus.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lütkenhöner and Steinsträter, 1998.

claim: Significant correlations were found between variability in ERP-measured N1–P2 complex and BOLD responses in several regions, including the primary and secondary auditory areas.
source: A more recent study (Mayhew et al., 2010) combined ERP and fMRI, and found significant correlations between variability in ERP-measured N1–P2 complex and BOLD responses in several regions, including the primary (Heschl's gyrus) and secondary (Planum Temporale and STG areas) auditory areas.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mayhew et al., 2010.

claim: Reports of previous studies asking whether primary and secondary auditory cortices manifest neuro-typical structure and function in dyslexia are mixed.
source: Reports of previous studies asking whether these areas manifest neuro-typical structure and function in dyslexia are mixed. For example, Clark et al. (2014) reported early anatomical abnormalities, whereas Boets et al. (2013) reported adequate stimulus resolution.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to conflicting studies (Clark et al., 2014 and Boets et al., 2013).

claim: Clark et al. (2014) reported early anatomical abnormalities in auditory cortices in dyslexia.
source: For example, Clark et al. (2014) reported early anatomical abnormalities, whereas Boets et al. (2013) reported adequate stimulus resolution.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Clark et al., 2014.

claim: Boets et al. (2013) reported adequate stimulus resolution in auditory cortices in dyslexia.
source: For example, Clark et al. (2014) reported early anatomical abnormalities, whereas Boets et al. (2013) reported adequate stimulus resolution.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Boets et al., 2013.

claim: The broad distribution of dyslexics' faster decay of adaptation is in line with recent observations of a domain general abnormally small adaptation in dyslexia.
source: The broad distribution of dyslexics' faster decay of adaptation is in line with recent observations of a domain general abnormally small adaptation in dyslexia (Perrachione et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Perrachione et al., 2016.

claim: Perrachione et al. (2016) found reduced stimulus-specific adaptation in the auditory, visual, and associative cortices in dyslexia.
source: The researchers compared BOLD responses to stimulus repetitions (in blocks of ~10 s) with BOLD response to non-repeated stimuli (auditory and visual), and found reduced stimulus-specific adaptation in the auditory (superior temporal), visual (fusiform and lateral occipital [LO]), and associative (insular and inferior frontal) cortices.
evidence: The claim is based on a description of findings from Perrachione et al., 2016.

claim: Perrachione et al. (2016) found a three-way interaction of group x condition x time, where controls' increase of adaptation along the block was larger than that of participants with dyslexia.
source: Importantly, they found a three-way interaction of group (control and dyslexic) x condition (repeated and non-repeated) x time (within the block), where controls' increase of adaptation along the block was larger than that of participants with dyslexia.
evidence: The claim is based on a description of findings from Perrachione et al., 2016.

claim: The timescale of impaired retention in dyslexia is slower than that of sensory memory (iconic or echoic memory is <<1 s).
source: We should note that the timescale of impaired retention in dyslexia is slower than that of sensory memory (iconic or echoic memory is <<1 s).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about sensory memory timescales.

claim: Impaired retention in dyslexia is expected to affect perception owing to reduced cross-trial retention.
source: Still, it is expected to affect the perception of individuals with dyslexia owing to their reduced cross-trial retention.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study's findings.

claim: Impaired retention in dyslexia is expected to impede performance in a broad range of perceptual tasks, such as entrainment to rapid stimuli, but only in protocols that contain stimulus repetitions.
source: It is therefore expected to impede their performance in a broad range of perceptual tasks, such as entrainment to rapid stimuli (e.g., Witton et al., 1998; Goswami, 2011; Lehongre et al., 2013), but only in protocols that contain stimulus repetitions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study's findings and supported by citations to related research.

claim: Listeners entrain better to familiar compared with unfamiliar stimuli.
source: Indeed, it was shown that listeners entrain better to familiar compared with unfamiliar stimuli (Doelling and Poeppel, 2015; Kumagai et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Doelling and Poeppel, 2015 and Kumagai et al., 2017.

claim: The advantage of familiarity is expected to be smaller in dyslexia.
source: The advantage of familiarity is expected to be smaller in dyslexia.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study's findings about faster decay of adaptation in dyslexia.

claim: The faster decay of implicit perceptual memory of individuals with dyslexia is expected to impede their long-term accumulation of stimulus statistics.
source: The faster decay of implicit perceptual memory of individuals with dyslexia is expected to also impede their long-term accumulation of stimulus statistics, and consequently to reduce the complexity and richness of their long-term accumulated categorical representations (e.g., Perrachione et al., 2011; Banai and Ahissar, 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study's findings and supported by citations to related research.

claim: The data point to the specific neural structures that underlie the 'anchoring deficit' in dyslexia.
source: In summary, the data collected in this study point to the specific neural structures that underlie the 'anchoring deficit' in dyslexia, namely a reduced use of stimulus statistics (Ahissar et al., 2006; Ahissar, 2007; Oganian and Ahissar, 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on the fMRI data collected in the study and supported by citations to the anchoring deficit hypothesis.

claim: The data suggest a broad multimodal cortical distribution that includes, but is not limited to, sensory areas.
source: These data suggest a broad multimodal (e.g., Jaffe-Dax et al., 2016) cortical distribution that includes, but is not limited to, sensory areas.
evidence: The claim is based on the fMRI data collected in the study and supported by a citation to Jaffe-Dax et al., 2016.

claim: In the two-tone frequency discrimination task, subjects were asked to indicate which of two sequentially presented tones had a higher pitch.
source: In the two-tone frequency discrimination task, subjects were asked to indicate which of two sequentially presented tones had a higher pitch.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental task used in the study.

claim: The tones were 50 ms long, presented at comfortable intensity, and were drawn from a uniform distribution between 800 Hz and 1250 Hz.
source: The tones were 50 ms long, presented at comfortable intensity, and were drawn from a uniform distribution between 800 Hz and 1250 Hz.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental parameters used in the study.

claim: The frequency difference within each pair was randomly drawn at between 1% and 20%.
source: The frequency difference within each pair was randomly drawn at between 1% and 20% (following the protocol in Jaffe-Dax et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental parameters used in the study.

claim: The TOAs used in this study (3, 6, 9, or 15 s) are longer than those in the previous ERP experiment (1.5, 3, 6, and 9 s).
source: These TOAs are longer than those in our previous ERP experiment (1.5, 3, 6, and 9 s, Jaffe-Dax et al., 2017), because the controls' ERP (N1 and P2) response at 9 s was still larger than that at 6 s.
evidence: The claim describes the methodological choice and is supported by reference to the previous study.

claim: The block design allowed measurement of the dynamics of adaptation in timescales that are independent of the sluggishness of typical hemodynamic response function (HRF).
source: The block design allowed us to measure the dynamics of adaptation in timescales that are independent of the sluggishness of typical hemodynamic response function (HRF), as we analyzed each block as a whole, and not on a trial-by-trial basis.
evidence: The claim explains the methodological rationale for the block design.

claim: The number of trials was too small for robust estimation of behavioral context effects.
source: However, the number of trials was too small for robust estimation of behavioral context effects, which are based on the difference in success rate (binary scores for each trial) between trials that gain and those that are hampered by the context (Jaffe-Dax et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on methodological limitations and supported by citation to the previous study.

claim: High-resolution T1-weighted MPRAGE images were acquired using a 3T Magnetom Skyra Siemens scanner and a 32-channel head coil.
source: Before the functional scan, high-resolution (1 × 1 × 1 mm resolution) T1-weighted magnetization-prepared rapid acquisition gradient-echo (MPRAGE) images were acquired using a 3T Magnetom Skyra Siemens scanner and a 32-channel head coil at the ELSC Neuroimaging Unit (ENU).
evidence: The claim describes the imaging methodology used in the study.

claim: The cortical surface was reconstructed from the high-resolution anatomical images using standard procedures implemented by the BrainVoyager QX software package.
source: The cortical surface was reconstructed from the high-resolution anatomical images using standard procedures implemented by the BrainVoyager QX software package (version 2.84; Brain Innovation, The Netherlands).
evidence: The claim describes the image processing methodology used in the study.

claim: Preprocessing of functional scans included 3D motion correction, slice scan time correction, and removal of low frequencies up to three cycles per scan.
source: Preprocessing of functional scans in BrainVoyager included 3D motion correction, slice scan time correction, and removal of low frequencies up to three cycles per scan (linear trend removal and high-pass filtering).
evidence: The claim describes the preprocessing steps used in the study.

claim: Each voxel's time course was z-score normalized and smoothed using a 3D Gaussian filter (FWHM of 4 mm).
source: Each voxel's time course was z-score normalized and smoothed using a 3D Gaussian filter (full width at half maximum [FWHM] of 4 mm).
evidence: The claim describes the preprocessing steps used in the study.

claim: A standard (two gamma) hemodynamic response function was convolved with the trial timings of each TOA block to build four predictors for the subsequent GLM analysis.
source: A standard (two gamma) hemodynamic response function (Friston et al., 1998) was convolved with the trial timings of each TOA block to build four predictors for the subsequent GLM analysis.
evidence: The claim describes the analysis methodology and is supported by a citation to Friston et al., 1998.

claim: Whole-brain significance results were corrected for multiple comparison false-positive biases by a Monte-Carlo cluster correction.
source: Whole-brain significance results were corrected for multiple comparison false-positive biases by a Monte-Carlo cluster correction (Forman et al., 1995), implemented using a plug-in of BrainVoyager (Goebel et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim describes the statistical correction method and is supported by citations to Forman et al., 1995 and Goebel et al., 2006.

claim: The Monte-Carlo procedure yielded a cluster threshold of 44 voxels for an a-priori chosen probability for type I error of 0.05.
source: The Monte-Carlo procedure was given an a-priori chosen probability for type I error of 0.05 and yielded a cluster threshold of 44 voxels.
evidence: The claim describes the statistical threshold used in the study.

claim: Non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney's U-test) were used for group comparisons.
source: Non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney's U-test) were used for group comparisons, as we did not assume a normal distribution, as in our previous study (Jaffe-Dax et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim describes the statistical method used and is supported by citation to the previous study.

claim: Adaptation is an automatic, implicit, and stimulus-specific decrease of the response to repeated stimuli.
source: The neural mechanism that may underlie the implicit learning of experimental statistics is adaptation; that is, an automatic, implicit, and stimulus-specific decrease of the response to repeated stimuli.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about neural adaptation.

claim: Contraction to the mean merges the implicit predicted stimulus (based on previous exposures) with the current sensory estimate, forming a coherent percept.
source: This contraction to the mean merges the (implicit) predicted stimulus (based on previous exposures) with the current sensory estimate, forming a coherent percept.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about perceptual mechanisms.

claim: The study used fast-acquisition fMRI to show the cortical distribution of abnormal dynamics of adaptation in dyslexia.
source: Here, we show the cortical distribution of these abnormal dynamics of adaptation using fast-acquisition fMRI.
evidence: The claim describes the main methodological approach of the study.

claim: Faster decay of adaptation in dyslexia is widespread, although the most significant effects are found in the left superior temporal lobe, including the auditory cortex.
source: We find that faster decay of adaptation in dyslexia is widespread, although the most significant effects are found in the left superior temporal lobe, including the auditory cortex.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: The broad distribution of faster decay of adaptation suggests that the faster decay of implicit memory of individuals with dyslexia is a general characteristic of their cortical dynamics.
source: This broad distribution suggests that the faster decay of implicit memory of individuals with dyslexia is a general characteristic of their cortical dynamics, which also affects sensory cortices.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study's findings.

claim: All cortical regions that responded to tone discrimination showed a tendency to decay faster in participants with dyslexia.
source: All cortical regions that responded to tone discrimination showed a tendency to decay faster in participants with dyslexia.
evidence: The claim summarizes a general finding from the data analysis.

claim: Whole-brain analysis revealed significant group differences in the left superior temporal lobe and in the right insular cortex.
source: Whole-brain analysis revealed significant group differences in the left superior temporal lobe and in the right insular cortex, and ROI analysis revealed significant differences in the left primary auditory cortex.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings from the whole-brain analysis.

claim: ROI analysis revealed significant differences in the left primary auditory cortex.
source: Whole-brain analysis revealed significant group differences in the left superior temporal lobe and in the right insular cortex, and ROI analysis revealed significant differences in the left primary auditory cortex.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings from the ROI analysis.

claim: The primary auditory cortex is composed of three sub-regions.
source: We used a combined cytoarchitectonic (Morosan et al., 2001) and myeloarchitectonic (Dick et al., 2012) definition of these areas (the primary auditory cortex being composed of three sub-regions and two secondary auditory areas [Planum Temporale and Planum Polare]).
evidence: The claim is based on established anatomical definitions supported by citations.

claim: None of the other sub-regions of auditory cortex yielded significant group differences.
source: None of the other sub-regions of auditory cortex yielded significant group differences.
evidence: The claim reports negative findings from the ROI analysis.

claim: The observation that controls' increase of adaptation along the block was larger than that of participants with dyslexia is fully consistent with the observation of dyslexics' faster decay of adaptation.
source: This observation, which results from controls' accumulative adaptation with stimulus repetition, is fully consistent with our observation of dyslexics' faster decay of adaptation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference connecting findings from Perrachione et al., 2016 with the current study.
